After the print run, a second web lifecycle rechecks the local binding on 2.5.0/2.5.1/2.5.2, sets `swarm_mode:false`, verifies the version-appropriate state proof, shuts down cleanly, and requires `swarm_mode.exit` in the main journal. Activation consumes part of the same finite job budget rather than extending it. `runSwarm` solely owns session deactivation: normal cleanup uses the remaining budget, while failure recovery has a separate two-second cancellation-aware bound and is never retried. Print/session failures stay primary, with exit codes and cleanup diagnostics preserved. Cancellation aborts the owned lifecycle and never starts a fresh cleanup server. Every post-mutation failure retains the session identity; process/group uncertainty is marked without inventing an ID; process groups are rechecked after teardown, unknown survivors are unverified, unproven groups are never signalled, and a same-PID/start-token process that changes PGID remains active but is not a validated signal target. Root loss requires a previously observed matching identity; first-missing roots and actual probe errors/timeouts remain unverified. Reparenting and PGID moves preserve the current verified child identity for revalidation rather than treating it as exited. Unverified cleanup prevents success and preserves raw output, structured diagnostics, and the write worktree for recovery.\n\nOlder certified versions keep the direct `kimi -p` path. The web processes are narrow, planned lifecycle helpers, not a second model runner and not a general RPC transport.\n\n## Read-only swarm (`/kimi:swarm`)\n\n`/kimi:swarm` (v1.2) fans a **read-only** review out across subagents using kimi-code's `AgentSwarm` tool (kimi-code 0.12.0+). The coordinator launches one subagent per target (file/module/question); each inspects the workspace with read tools and reports findings, which the coordinator consolidates into one markdown report. It opens **zero new write surface**.\n\n- **The hook label is `swarm`, and it allows the read-only tool set PLUS `AgentSwarm`.** The coordinator must be allowed to call `AgentSwarm` (else the swarm never launches), but no write/edit/shell tool is allowed. The exact allowed tool name is `AgentSwarm` (verified at 0.42.0 against `packages/agent-core-v2/src/features/swarm/tools/agent-swarm/agentSwarmTool.ts`: `'AgentSwarm'`, strict schema). The singular `Agent` tool is deliberately *not* allowed — swarm is the fan-out surface, not arbitrary delegation.\n- **Every subagent inherits the `swarm` label and fires the same hook.** On native v2 (0.42.0) `AgentSwarm` children run in-process in a child DI scope with their OWN eager external-hooks service, so every child tool call passes the same before-execute channel and the same managed hook — there is no sub-vs-main branch and no deny-all shortcut on the swarm route. So a subagent's `Write`/`Edit`/`Bash` is denied exactly like a single-turn review's. The swarm listener in that channel is non-terminal and nothing auto-approves `AgentSwarm` ahead of the hook. (Legacy-v1 ≤ 0.41 reached the same result by placing the hook policy at index 0 of every agent's permission stack.) **Required for final certification evidence** (`tests/runtime/real-binary-smoke.test.ts`, run via `bun run smoke:real`): distinct child journals must exist, and each assigned Write/Edit `path` must be correlated through its `toolCallId` with the managed denial in that exact tool result; unrelated denials and coordinator-only reports are insufficient. On 2.3.2, 2.3.3, 2.4.0, 2.4.1, 2.5.0, 2.5.1 and 2.5.2, targeted controls also prove that direct OFF produces no children while the preactivated ON path produces the real child journals and denials.\n- **The managed hook is the read-only boundary; no `explore`-profile second layer is assumed.** Production deliberately omits `subagent_type` for read-only swarm rather than selecting kimi-code's `explore` profile. Every coordinator and subagent tool call is enforced by the same managed hook.\n- **Swarm refuses without the hook, like every model-spawning command.** A swarm makes the reason especially acute: it asks for up to `--cap` subagents, but this total-count hint is advisory, so a missing hook would remove enforcement from all of them at once. `KIMI_PLUGIN_CC_SKIP_HOOK_CHECK=1` remains an explicit tests/diagnostics escape hatch, not a recovery path.\n- **The only new risk is COST, and the plugin bounds it.** Read-only swarm writes nothing, so the new risk is runaway cost from N parallel model runs (and possible nested `AgentSwarm`). `/kimi:swarm` enforces a **mandatory finite wall-clock ceiling** via its AbortController (`--budget`, default 30m); the SIGTERM→SIGKILL descendant-reaping cancellation reaps the whole subagent process tree. Two **distinct** subagent bounds: `--cap N` is a *soft* prompt-injected hint on TOTAL subagent count (the hook is stateless and cannot enforce a count, so the model may exceed it), and `--max-concurrency N` is a *hard* ceiling on how many subagents kimi-code's `SubagentBatch` runs concurrently — exported as `KIMI_CODE_AGENT_SWARM_MAX_CONCURRENCY` (PR #888) on **kimi-code 0.18.0+** (older binaries ignore the unknown env var, so on < 0.18 only the soft hint applies). It **defaults to 4** when the user passes none (`resolveSwarmMaxConcurrency` in swarm.ts), so every swarm run — agent-dispatched or human-typed — carries an enforced peak-parallelism ceiling on 0.18.0+ rather than falling back to kimi-code's internal ramp; pass an explicit value to widen or throttle. **Never merge them into one flag:** concurrency ≠ total count — a hard concurrency cap of N still permits more than N subagents over the life of the run, just never more than N at once. The `--budget` bounds elapsed time, not a dollar amount or total token count; `--max-concurrency` bounds *peak* parallelism (the spike in simultaneous model spend), and `--cap` is only an advisory total-count nudge. Folding both onto one flag would create the \"cap-as-total-count illusion\" — a user reading `--cap N` would expect a total bound but receive only a peak-parallelism one.\n- **A model-invocable `kimi-swarm` agent (v1.3) wraps this command.** The `/kimi:swarm` slash command is human-only (`disable-model-invocation: true`, the blanket convention for *all* commands), but the `kimi-swarm` subagent lets the main thread *dispatch* a read-only fan-out on its own judgement — the same human-command + model-invocable-agent split that `kimi-review`/`kimi-challenge`/`kimi-ask`/`kimi-rescue` already use. Swarm is a safe candidate for an agent precisely because it is **read-only (zero write surface)**: the only thing auto-dispatch adds is COST exposure, already bounded by the hard `--budget` and a hard `--max-concurrency` that the runtime now defaults to 4 for every swarm run (enforced on 0.18.0+) — so an auto-dispatched fan-out is bounded by construction, not by ignorable agent prose (the agent additionally restricts backgrounding to explicit user requests). `/kimi:pursue` ALSO gains a model-invocable agent (`kimi-pursue`, v1.3 — see the Autonomous goal mode section above): it is write-capable, but auto-dispatch widens no write surface (the rescue workspace allowlist + the managed PreToolUse hook gate every tool call on every continuation turn, and it cannot mutate git state) and removes no bound (the mandatory `--budget` ceiling holds), so its agent path is exactly as confined as its command path. Because it is the plugin's highest-autonomy surface, its agent description demands an explicit hands-off-autonomy request and steers single bounded tasks to `kimi-rescue`.\n\n## Write-capable swarm (`/kimi:swarm --write`)\n\n`/kimi:swarm --write` (v1.4) is the first WRITE mode for swarm: the coordinator and `coder` (write-capable) subagents EDIT files in parallel. It is **designed to keep direct edits in a throwaway Git worktree, subject to the test-runner trust boundary above**, and the result is handed back as a patch the user reviews before anything touches their branch.\n\n- **One ephemeral worktree for the whole swarm (Design A).** kimi-code runs `AgentSwarm` subagents **in-process**, all sharing the coordinator's session workspace (at 0.42.0 a child DI scope under `features/swarm/`; pre-0.42 `subagent-host.ts:362`, `cwd: parent.config.cwd`) — so \"a worktree per subagent\" is impossible without abandoning `AgentSwarm`. Instead the plugin creates ONE detached worktree off HEAD (under its own data dir, never inside the user repo) and spawns the coordinator `kimi -p` with cwd = that worktree. Every subagent inherits it. The worktree is disposable: a botched run is thrown away.\n- **Writes are confined by the hook to a forge-proof trusted root.** The `swarm-write` hook label routes write/edit/shell through the **rescue allowlist verbatim** (workspace check, symlink/realpath reject, mutating-flag + exec-delegating-flag detector, git-mutation deny), but scoped to `KIMI_PLUGIN_CC_WORKSPACE_ROOT` — the worktree path the plugin exports on the spawn — **NOT** the hook payload `cwd`. The model running inside kimi cannot set an env var on its already-spawned process, so confinement does not depend on how upstream derives the payload cwd for an in-process subagent. A missing trusted root **fails closed** (all writes denied). An out-of-worktree write (absolute path into the user's real tree) is rejected by the allowlist's `isWithin` check; a write to the worktree's `.git` pointer is rejected by the `.git`-segment check.\n- **`coder` subagents really can write, and the hook is the sole boundary.** Verified at kimi-code 0.42.0: swarm subagents get their own eager external-hooks service under the standard before-execute channel — there is no deny-all path on the swarm route (the `btw` side-question path is separate). Write-swarm's `coder` subagents DO have edit tools, and the managed PreToolUse hook is the **only** write boundary — which is why the trusted-root confinement above is load-bearing and gated tightly.\n- **The plugin never touches git; the main thread owns the merge.** Subagents cannot run git (allowlist denies mutation). The plugin captures the change set with `git add -N` (intent-to-add, so new files appear in the diff WITHOUT writing loose objects into the shared object DB) + `git diff --binary` (untruncated, applyable), writes it to a `swarm-write-<jobId>.patch` artifact, and prints the path. It does **not** `git apply`, commit, or move any ref — the user/main thread reviews the patch and applies it (`git apply <path>`). The worktree shares the main repo's object DB and refs, but no ref/HEAD is ever moved, so the user's repository state is untouched.\n- **The patch is captured on every terminal path, before cleanup.** Success, cancel, budget-expiry, and failure all capture the (possibly partial) patch BEFORE `git worktree remove --force` discards the tree, so a cancelled run never silently loses the work the subagents already did. If capture itself fails, the job fails instead of completing and the worktree is retained with its path in the error details for recovery. That guarantee covers the plugin's own terminal paths, including `companion.sh cancel`. It does **not** cover a harness interrupt: Esc/TaskStop delivers SIGTERM then SIGKILL after ~1.35s (measured, process-group-wide), which is shorter than the 1500ms child escalation plus quiescence plus patch capture — so a hard interrupt can kill the companion mid-teardown and lose the patch. `companion.sh cancel` signals from a separate process not racing that deadline and is the work-preserving stop. Abandoned worktrees are retained, never age-deleted. Use the preview/apply recovery procedure in [swarm-recovery.md](swarm-recovery.md); uncertain ownership refuses automatic cleanup.\n- **Gated tightly.** Requires kimi-code **≥ 0.18.0** (below it `KIMI_CODE_AGENT_SWARM_MAX_CONCURRENCY` is ignored, so a write fan-out would have no hard peak bound — unacceptable for concurrent writers); because that cap cannot be guaranteed without a confirmed version, the write-mode version gate **fails closed** on an unconfirmable `kimi --version` probe (the shared execution-plan gate also refuses unverified or uncertified binaries for read-only swarm; older certified legacy versions may lack the hard concurrency setting). Also requires a git repo with a **committed HEAD**, and the PreToolUse hook (**refuses** without it, like read swarm). Bases the worktree on HEAD, so a **loud warning** fires when the working tree is dirty (uncommitted work is not visible to the swarm). Default `--max-concurrency` is **1** (serialize) since disjoint-target partitioning is prompt-only and unenforceable by the stateless hook; the coordinator prompt also forbids git mutation and nested `AgentSwarm`.\n- **Required for final certification evidence.** `tests/runtime/real-binary-smoke.test.ts` runs the real `runSwarm --write` and requires the POSITIVE end-to-end: distinct child journals contain their assigned edits with `Write`/`Replaced` results on the same `toolCallId`, those child-authored changes land in the worktree and captured patch, the user's real tree is byte-identical + git-clean, and the worktree is cleaned up. A patch without per-call child provenance is not accepted as fan-out evidence. The NEGATIVE lane correlates each absolute out-of-root `path` and `toolCallId` with its managed denial. It is the check that catches `tool_input` field-name drift — `Write`/`Edit` carry `path`, not `file_path`, and reading the wrong key denies every real write silently.\n- **Model-invocable agent (v1.5), patch-only by construction.** Following the field-proof above, `--write` now has a `kimi-swarm-write` subagent so the main thread can dispatch a write fan-out on its own judgement — the same human-command + model-invocable-agent split the rest of the suite uses. Auto-dispatch is a safe extension here because it widens **no** write surface and removes **no** bound: the agent path runs the identical `runSwarm --write` code, so edits still land only in the throwaway worktree, the managed hook still gates every `coder` subagent, the patch is still handed back for the user to apply (**the plugin never applies or commits**), and `--budget` + default `--max-concurrency` 1 + the hook requirement all still hold. In fact write-swarm is a *less* dangerous agent than the `kimi-pursue` agent already shipped: pursue writes directly into the workspace, whereas write-swarm's output is a patch the human reviews before anything reaches a real tree. Because it is still a write surface, the agent description demands BOTH signals — many disjoint write targets AND explicit fan-out intent — and steers single edits to `kimi-rescue`, read-only fan-outs to `kimi-swarm`, and autonomous loops to `kimi-pursue`. Default `--max-concurrency` stays **1**; raising it (concurrent writers) remains a deliberate, human-or-explicitly-requested choice.\n\n## MCP transport and long-running jobs\n\nThe plugin also bundles an MCP stdio server for Claude Code and Codex. This is an additive transport, not a second execution engine or a way around the managed hook. The seven model tools run the same certified companion operations, exact-version checks, native-v2 preflight, workspace allowlists, finite budgets, and artifact rendering as the slash commands and skills. The review gate remains a separate Stop-hook feature.\n\nClaude Code task-capable calls return durable MCP task IDs and use `tasks/get` and `tasks/cancel`. Codex currently consumes ordinary MCP tool results, not this task extension: after attachment, model tools return a job handle when the job is still running or its terminal result when already settled. `kimi_job_status`, `kimi_job_result`, and `kimi_job_cancel` provide polling and cancellation. Do not describe the Codex path as native MCP tasks.\n\nClaude supplies its project directory as the default workspace. A configured host workspace is a containment boundary: an explicit workspace must be that directory or a descendant, not an arbitrary override. Codex calls normally supply an absolute `workspace` on the initial operation because its packaged stdio server runs from the plugin root; that explicit path is the operation's trust choice. Subsequent job control can use the persisted binding. Job controls manage only MCP-launched jobs, require the same canonical workspace and repository, and cannot inspect or cancel an arbitrary CLI job by ID.\n\nAttachment waits for the operation to install cancellation handlers, with a 60-second bound. Verified teardown can close a stalled launch; missing identity or inconclusive termination evidence keeps it starting and recoverable by ID. `kimi_pid` is recorded at actual spawn rather than inferred from a later process-list match.\n\nThe MCP task/job ID is preassigned and bound to the job's real `operation_kind`, not merely its lineage. `mcp_tasks` stores launch and ownership metadata; the normal `jobs` table remains the outcome authority. Failed jobs, including budget timeouts, produce completed tasks with `isError:true` and the failed-job artifact, so partial output is not mistaken for a final answer. Supervisor and protocol failures are distinct from ordinary Kimi failures.\n\nClosing an MCP connection does not cancel work. A later server reopens the same store and resumes status/result handling by ID. Generic stale sweeps skip MCP-owned rows, and direct CLI cancellation refuses them; use MCP job controls for those jobs. Companion and observed Kimi-descendant identities include start tokens and process groups; MCP cancellation and stale cleanup revalidate them rather than signalling a recycled PID. Cancellation remains cooperative and does not roll back edits. Pursue teardown and write-swarm patch capture still run through the existing companion path; write-swarm captures its patch on every terminal path before removing the worktree.\n\n## Response budgets and partial output (2.2.0)\n\nEvery single-turn command runs under a wall-clock budget: ask, review and\nchallenge default to 30 minutes, rescue to 45, and `--budget <dur>` (at most\n24h) overrides it per job. The budget is persisted on the job row, so a detached\nworker and a same-operation resume use the same ceiling. For these commands the\nbudget is a response-time limit, not a safety bound: a timeout is a safe\nfailure. The job stays `failed`; whatever assistant prose had settled is written\ninto the artifact under a heading that says it is NOT a final answer, and\n`result <jobId> --json` reports `partial_output: true` when prose exists.\nCancellation and nonzero exits do not capture partial output. A session ID is kept if Kimi announced it or, on a native-v2 budget timeout, recovered from the session store when exactly one session matches this spawn — created between spawn and settlement in the same directory AND whose journal opens with this job's exact prompt; `result --json` identifies the source in `kimi_session_id_source`, and `error.details.session_recovery` says why no ID was recovered (`none`, `journal_missing:<n>`, `digest_mismatch:<n>`, `ambiguous:<n>`, `enumeration_capped`, `engine_unobserved`). Recovery is bounded and refuses ambiguity, incomplete enumeration, and IDs already used by another job on this host. The prompt binding is what makes attribution proof rather than probability: a concurrent interactive session in the same directory, another host's finished job (host stores cannot see each other's IDs) or a `state.json` planted by repository code running under rescue all fail it unless they carry the exact prompt, and a planted clean journal could otherwise replay attacker-written turns into the next resume. Recovery is skipped when the run never emitted the `system.version` marker, since resume would refuse the row as lineage-unknown anyway. Recovered sessions still require proven native-v2 lineage and the raw plan-taint scan before resume. Inherited budgets are printed to stderr at launch; status and `result --json` expose `budget_source` (`explicit`, `inherited`, or `default`; old non-null budgets report `unknown`).\n\nPursue and swarm keep their ceilings as the sole hard bound on autonomy and\ncost. One nuance: a run whose process exits cleanly in the same event-loop tick\nas the budget timer is accepted as a success rather than discarded, so a goal\ncan complete at most one tick past its ceiling — teardown has already settled by\nthen, and nothing runs longer.\n\nEvery spawn also deletes `KIMI_CODE_TRUST_WORKSPACE` from the child\nenvironment (kimi-code 2.2.0): a trusted workspace boots repo-defined project\nMCP servers at bootstrap, outside the PreToolUse hook, and an inherited value\nwould have trusted every plugin spawn including swarm-write's throwaway\nworktree. A directory the operator trusted interactively in the Kimi TUI still\nhas that property; that persisted-trust route is a documented residual, not\nsomething the plugin can close.\n\nPlugin-managed execution must remain local. Unused remote declarations can remain in operator config, but a configured remote default refuses before spawn. Disabling workspace trust through `[workspace] require_trust = false` also refuses, because it would enable project MCP outside the managed hook. Launcher environment selectors are reserved. Fresh exact 2.5.0/2.5.1/2.5.2 print selects `--environment local`; resume instead inspects persisted metadata and every agent journal and refuses nonlocal or wrong-root records against the expected execution root (the isolated worktree for swarm-write); older sessions without environment records do not fail this check merely for lacking them.\n\n## Running a newer Kimi than the plugin certifies\n\nThe plugin refuses any kimi-code version it has not certified, so an operator\nwho tracks `@latest` loses every `/kimi:*` command until the next certification.\nThe clean way to have both is to give the plugin its own binary: install the\nhighest certified version somewhere stable and point `KIMI_PLUGIN_CC_KIMI_BIN`\nat it (the runtime resolves that path instead of `kimi` on `PATH`; every spawn\nstill exports `KIMI_CODE_NO_AUTO_UPDATE=1`, so the pinned copy never drifts).\n\n```sh\nPIN=~/.local/share/kimi-plugin-cc/kimi-bin/2.5.2\nmkdir -p \"$PIN\" && cd \"$PIN\" && printf '{\"name\":\"kimi-plugin-cc-pin\",\"private\":true}\\n' > package.json\nnpm install @moonshot-ai/kimi-code@2.5.2\nexport KIMI_PLUGIN_CC_KIMI_BIN=\"$PIN/node_modules/.bin/kimi\"   # e.g. in ~/.zshenv\n```\n\nBoth binaries share `~/.kimi-code` (login, config, hook), so nothing else\nchanges. The certified maximum can be read from the installed plugin\n(`NATIVE_V2_CERTIFIED_VERSIONS` in `dist/kimi-engine.js`), which lets an upgrade\nscript bump the pin automatically after each certification.\n\n## The setup probe\n\n`/kimi:setup` runs a two-layer probe before reporting success:\n\n1. **Direct probe.** Spawns the hook with the same Node binary (`process.execPath`) the companion is running under. Sends synthetic PreToolUse stdin with `KIMI_PLUGIN_CC_CMD=review` + a Bash tool request. Asserts exit 2 + non-empty stderr.\n2. **Shell probe.** Re-runs the same payload via `/bin/sh -c \"<command>\"` — the exact spawn shape kimi-code's hook runner uses. Same assertion.\n\nBoth must pass. The shell probe catches the case where `process.execPath` works but `/bin/sh` can't resolve the path through quoting (a `KIMI_PLUGIN_CC_NODE_BIN` override pointing at a binary in a shell-unsafe path, for example). If either probe fails, setup reports failure with the captured stderr and the user can act on a clear signal rather than discover the gap by accident.\n\n## How to verify the install yourself\n\n```\n/kimi:setup --check\n```\n\nReports the current state without writing. The output line you want to see is `Probe: ok`. If the probe is failing, the `Details:` section shows which layer failed and what stderr was captured.\n\n`/kimi:setup --check` is strict and exits nonzero on failure. It rejects an unloadable TOML file, any invalid configured hook, and any managed block that doesn't pass the [`parseManagedBlock`](../runtime/hooks/managed-block.ts) grammar (missing `[[hooks]]` table, wrong event, present `matcher = ...` line, duplicate blocks, orphan markers, or a stale hook-script path). `/kimi:setup` (without `--check`) can replace a malformed managed block, but it will not overwrite or silently work around invalid foreign config: if the complete candidate file would not load, setup leaves the existing file unchanged and identifies the bad hook or TOML line.\n\nIn Codex, ask `$kimi-setup` to check the active installation. Use its sanitized output for routine diagnosis. Do not print raw `config.toml` or OAuth files: they can contain credentials. Missing comment markers alone do not mean the hook is missing; the verifier also accepts a valid marker-less entry.\n\nFollow the reported remedy. Only run setup and retry automatically when `retryable_after_setup` is literally `true` and setup succeeds.\n\n## How to opt out\n\n```\n/kimi:setup --uninstall\n```\n\nRemoves the managed block from `~/.kimi-code/config.toml`. Subsequent kimi-plugin-cc command invocations:\n\n- Every model-spawning command will refuse before Kimi starts with its command-specific `*_HOOK_NOT_INSTALLED` error.\n- The review gate will skip visibly and allow the host to stop; it will not run an un-enforced model turn.\n\nFor tests or deliberate diagnostics only, `KIMI_PLUGIN_CC_SKIP_HOOK_CHECK=1` bypasses verification.\n\nThis diagnostic option bypasses hook verification only. It does not disable an installed hook or bypass engine certification, provenance checks, or the native-v2 preflight. Never use it to repair a failed setup.\n\n## Refusal codes of the native-v2 contract (v1.10.0)\n\nEvery refusal below is raised BEFORE a kimi process is created (or, for the provenance mismatch, before any record reaches the caller) and is **not** repaired by `/kimi:setup` — the remedy is the named setting, binary, or a fresh session. Agents must not retry through setup on these. Every row says so explicitly with `retryable_after_setup: false` in `details` (since 1.10.1; in 1.10.0 `CLI_V2_HOOK_ORDER_UNSAFE`, `INVALID_ENV` and the legacy-v1 form of `KIMI_CAPABILITY_NOT_CERTIFIED` omitted it). The retry gate keys on the field being literally `true`, so an ABSENT field is treated as non-retryable — wrappers must do the same and never assert the field's presence.\n\n| Code | Raised when | Remedy |\n|---|---|---|\n| `KIMI_CAPABILITY_NOT_CERTIFIED` | the probed `kimi --version` is not in the operation's exact certified set (for example, an interactive CLI update installed an uncertified version) | update kimi-plugin-cc to a release certifying that version, or point `KIMI_PLUGIN_CC_KIMI_BIN` at a certified binary |\n| `CLI_V2_PLAN_MODE_CONFIGURED` | `<KIMI_CODE_HOME>/config.toml` sets the default-plan-mode key (any spelling normalizing to `defaultPlanMode`) to anything but literal `false` | set it to `false` or remove it |\n| `CLI_V2_CONFIG_UNREADABLE` | that config cannot be read safely (symlink, oversized, unparseable TOML, I/O error) — plan mode cannot be verified off | fix or remove the unreadable file |\n| `CLI_V2_EXPERIMENTAL_UNSAFE` | `[experimental] tower` / `subagent_fork` (config) or `KIMI_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_TOWER` / `…_SUBAGENT_FORK` (env) is truthy | unset the listed selector(s) |\n| `CLI_V2_HOOK_ORDER_UNSAFE` | the master `KIMI_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_FLAG` is truthy (`1|true|yes|on`) | unset it |\n| `KIMI_SESSION_PLAN_TAINTED` | the session to resume has a `plan_mode.*`/`plan.*` record in any agent `wire.jsonl` | start a fresh session (nothing saved is modified) |\n| `KIMI_SESSION_JOURNAL_UNAVAILABLE` | the session's journals cannot be found or read safely (missing dir, symlinked entry, oversized, not a regular file) | start a fresh session |\n| `KIMI_SESSION_LINEAGE_UNKNOWN` | the job to resume has no proven engine provenance, no recorded source job, or a source that owns a different session | start a fresh session; the old job's status/result/replay remain available |\n| `KIMI_SESSION_ENGINE_MISMATCH` | the source session ran on a different engine than the selected one | start a fresh session |\n| `CLI_ENGINE_PROVENANCE_MISMATCH` | the started engine contradicts the plan: no leading `system.version` marker on a v2 plan, a marker on a v1 plan, a marker whose version is malformed or ≠ the probed version, or any line (meta, unknown-role, malformed) ahead of the marker | the process tree is torn down before any record is delivered; check for a binary swap (`KIMI_PLUGIN_CC_KIMI_BIN`, auto-update) |\n| `INVALID_ENV` (`reserved_flag`) | `KIMI_PLUGIN_CC_KIMI_PREFIX_ARGS` carries a kimi root flag (session, prompt, permission/plan, model/profile/roots, or `-V`/`-h`) — the prefix is a launcher shim only | remove the flag from the prefix |\n\n## What this safety story does NOT cover\n\n- **Repository Git configuration and internal subprocesses.** The managed hook gates tool calls, not every internal subprocess. Upstream's explorer profile builds Git context with `git status` and `git log` outside the child tool hook. On 2.0.2 and 2.1.1, repository settings such as `core.fsmonitor` can execute a helper there, including during read-only swarm startup. Version 2.1.0 hardens these Git invocations; 2.1.1 rolls that hardening back to the previously certified behavior. Use trusted repositories and Git configuration. Certification does not establish a sandbox for hostile repositories or arbitrary Git helpers.\n- **Malicious kimi-code binaries.** The threat model assumes the user trusts the kimi-code binary they installed. A hostile binary can ignore the hook entry in its own config.\n- **TOCTOU between path check and edit.** The rescue allowlist resolves and checks paths at allowlist time. Between that check and the actual file write, an attacker with workspace write access could swap a symlink. The mitigation is workspace-write-trust — if untrusted code can edit your workspace, you have bigger problems than this plugin.\n- **Custom kimi-code skill libraries that bypass the hook.** Hooks fire on tool calls, not on skill activations. A skill that calls `Bash` will be hooked; a skill that performs file ops via a Node binding that doesn't surface as a tool call won't be. The default kimi-code skill catalog uses the standard tool surface.\n- **The calling host.** The plugin constrains its Kimi subprocesses. Claude Code and Codex have their own tool permissions; this hook does not govern the host's other tools.\n- **Compute exhaustion (no per-turn step cap on kimi-code ≥ 0.6.0).** kimi-code 0.6.0 (PR #186) removed the default 1000-step-per-turn ceiling; absent an explicit `max_steps_per_turn` in config, a turn can loop tool calls without an upstream bound. This is **not a write bypass** — every tool call still passes the PreToolUse hook and (for rescue) the workspace allowlist. The plugin bounds wall-clock and reaps the descendant process tree via its AbortController budget + SIGTERM→SIGKILL cancellation, so a runaway `/kimi:rescue` is cancellable; but if you want a hard step ceiling, set `max_steps_per_turn` in your kimi-code config.\n- **A poisoned `KIMI_MODEL_*` child environment.** kimi-code 0.6.0 (PR #212) added an opt-in env channel: when `KIMI_MODEL_NAME` is set, kimi synthesizes a provider (base URL + API key) as the default model. `kimi -p` inherits the plugin's parent environment, so a pre-poisoned `KIMI_MODEL_BASE_URL`/`KIMI_MODEL_API_KEY` could reroute model traffic (which may carry workspace file contents from review/ask). The plugin does not sanitize the child environment — this is the same parent-env trust the host already extends. It does **not** touch hook or permission config: kimi-code only writes the synthesized provider/model/thinking entries (never `hooks`), and strips them on any config write-back, so `/kimi:setup`'s managed hook block can neither clobber nor be clobbered by it.\n- **Out-of-band binary drift (kimi-code self-upgrades by default on ≥ 0.8.0).** kimi-code 0.8.0 (PR #334) added background automatic upgrades, enabled by default (`autoInstall: true`). The plugin's own `kimi -p` spawns are unaffected — in print mode the install source is forced `unsupported`, so a plugin spawn never swaps the binary mid-flight — but a user who *also* runs the interactive `kimi` TUI can be silently upgraded to a kimi-code the plugin has not compat-audited. This is a *version-assurance* boundary, not permission to guess. Setup emits an \"outside tested range\" warning and can complete, while every model-spawning command independently probes the exact command tuple and refuses an uncertified version before Kimi starts (`KIMI_CAPABILITY_NOT_CERTIFIED`; certification is per EXACT version on native v2 and per minor on legacy-v1). Update the plugin to a release that certifies the new version or point `KIMI_PLUGIN_CC_KIMI_BIN` at a certified binary; `KIMI_PLUGIN_CC_SKIP_VERSION_PROBE` is tests/smoke only. The current native-v2 versions are listed at the start of this guide. Legacy-v1 uses the tested minors through 0.41.x, with per-operation minimums, for an explicitly pinned binary. Every spawn probes the exact tuple and refuses an uncertified version (`KIMI_CAPABILITY_NOT_CERTIFIED`, see the refusal-code table above).\n- **New permission approval hook events are observability, not a decision surface.** kimi-code 0.8.0 (PR #336) added `PermissionRequest`/`PermissionResult` hook events. A user *can* register `[[hooks]]` blocks for them in `config.toml`, but they fire fire-and-forget (the result is discarded) and only inside the interactive approval/ask path — which `kimi -p` auto mode shadows. They **cannot** approve a tool the PreToolUse hook denied, cannot run on the plugin's `-p` path, and live in a disjoint event bucket from the managed `PreToolUse` block (no impersonation). Setup validates every configured hook against the reviewed schema for the probed CLI version. Version 2.0.0 has an explicitly reviewed schema; unknown major-version schemas fail closed.\n\n## Known limitation: Node version manager switches\n\nThe verifier does exact equality on the installed `command = \"...\"` against the canonical command built by `runtime/hooks/install-paths.ts`. It prefers a stable absolute Node path when that path resolves to the running interpreter. If you use `nvm`, `asdf`, `mise`, or `fnm` and switch the active Node version after `/kimi:setup`, the canonical command's Node binary path changes and the verifier rejects the previously-installed block. Every model-spawning command will refuse; the review gate will skip.\n\nThe workaround is to re-run `/kimi:setup` after any Node version switch. The strict behavior is deliberate — loosening the exact-equality check to \"survive\" Node moves would reopen the crafted-command bypass the audit closed (reports 27/28), so it stays strict by design.\n\n**Soft-recovery (H4):** to make that strict failure *legible* instead of cryptic, the verifier classifies a command mismatch when the block is otherwise valid. Rather than dumping the raw expected-vs-got command, it reports the drift class — e.g. *\"Node binary drift: the installed hook pins `/opt/homebrew/Cellar/node/26.0.0/bin/node`, which no longer exists on disk (this companion runs `…/26.3.0/…`) — the classic Node-upgrade / version-manager drift … Run /kimi:setup to re-pin\"*, or *\"Hook script path drift … likely a plugin update or move\"* when the version-stamped plugin path moved instead. A gone interpreter is the unambiguous signal. The same classified reason surfaces from `/kimi:setup --check`. This changes only the message; the strict installed/not-installed decision is unchanged.\n\n**Stable Node path (v1.9.0).** `process.execPath` is fully symlink-resolved, so under Homebrew it names `…/Cellar/node/<version>/bin/node` — a path that changes on every `brew upgrade node` and therefore invalidated **both** hosts' blocks at once, with no user-visible cause. `resolveNodeBinary` now prefers `process.argv0` (the name the interpreter was actually invoked with; `companion.sh` resolves `node` through the stable `/opt/homebrew/bin/node` symlink), **but only when that path is absolute AND `realpath`-identical to `process.execPath`**. The guard is the safety argument: the substitution can pick a more stable *name* for the interpreter already running, and provably never a *different* binary. Any doubt falls back to `execPath`. Exact-equality verification, absolute-path enforcement, and the shell probe are unchanged. It also keeps hook and companion on one interpreter by construction — previously the companion could run a freshly upgraded Node while the hook stayed pinned to a Cellar path `brew` had deleted, which fails to spawn and (exit 127) is read as **allow**. Version-manager users (nvm/asdf/mise/fnm) expose version-stamped paths directly, so `argv0 === execPath` and the limitation above still applies to them unchanged.\n\n## Hook-path drift is repaired by the caller, never by the verifier (v1.9.0)\n\nPlugin install paths are version-stamped (`…/kimi-marketplace/kimi/<version>/dist/hooks/approval-hook.js`), so a plugin update moves the hook script and the recorded command stops matching. That refusal is correct and fail-closed, but it is also routine, so refusals now carry a **machine-readable** classification alongside the prose reason:\n\n`HookInstallStatus.drift` = `{axis: \"hook-script\" | \"node-bin\" | \"both\", installedCommand, expectedCommand}`, surfaced in every refusal's `RuntimeError.details` as `drift_axis` / `retryable_after_setup`. It is populated **only** when a structurally sound block's command names different paths, and is derived **after** byte-exact equality has already failed — it can never influence the installed decision, exactly like the H4 prose classification. Refusals that re-pinning cannot fix (unresolvable command, unreadable config, invalid hook set, duplicate/orphan markers, missing script) carry no drift at all.\n\nAgents use `retryable_after_setup`, not `drift_axis` alone. They run setup for the affected host and retry once only when that field is literally `true` and setup exits successfully. This includes a moved hook script and a Node path spelling change proven to name the same interpreter. A different interpreter is not automatically retryable. `node-bin-not-executable` requires fixing the reported Node path; setup alone is not its remedy.\n\n**The verifier never repairs the config itself.** An in-verifier auto-repin was specified and rejected after two independent adversarial reviews found: a lock self-deadlock (the repin path and the install transaction both take a non-reentrant lock); a false \"target cannot be steered\" premise (`KIMI_PLUGIN_CC_HOOK_SCRIPT`/`NODE_BIN`/`HOST_ID` override resolution, and every proposed gate reads the same env, so they corroborate nothing); no version-monotonicity bound, letting a stale session pin the *global* block down to a pre-1.0.3 hook carrying the CRITICAL exec-delegation bypass; and a write→spawn TOCTOU in which one session repins to a deleted path inside another's spawn window, producing exit 127 → allow → an unenforced `rescue` run. Keeping repair in the caller makes it a **visible, permission-gated action in the transcript** instead of a silent mutation of a security surface. Full analysis: `.claude/hook-pin-durability-spec-2026-07-25.md`.\n\n## Reporting safety issues\n\nIf you find a way to coax /kimi:review, /kimi:challenge, /kimi:review_gate, or /kimi:ask into running a non-read tool — or to make /kimi:rescue mutate `.git/` or escape the workspace — please open a GitHub security advisory rather than a public issue.\n\n## Hook-escape monitor: detection evidence\n\n**Hook-escape monitor** (§1): the cli-client replays the pure hook policy on every streamed `tool_calls` entry; a call the policy denies whose tool result is not the hook's denial (byte-exact, or with upstream's repeat-breaker `<system-reminder>` decoration / handoff text) is recorded as `mismatch`, and a denied call still without a result at settlement as `unresolved`. Findings are **detection evidence, never a failure**: logged (`hook_escape`), persisted on the job row (`hook_escapes`, JSON), exposed by `status`/`result --json`, printed as a stderr `safety hook notice`, and carried in timeout details; the run continues, the job's outcome is unchanged, and the review gate stays fail-open and only annotates. The stream has no outcome field, so a mismatch is equally an upstream pre-hook rejection (unknown tool, disabled tool, invalid args, sensitive path, per-tool resolve errors), a coexisting hook or permission policy blocking first, or hook drift — failing the job needs positive execution evidence this stream does not provide. Streamed calls under read-only labels are covered (swarm subagents are in-process, not streamed); write labels only for the pure denials (plan/goal tools).\n\nA denied attempt alone is not a finding: the hook's denial text in the corresponding tool result (byte-exact, or carrying upstream's repeat-breaker decoration) proves enforcement and clears it. Anything else is recorded as `mismatch` with a 200-character excerpt; a denied call with no result at settlement as `unresolved`. **What a finding means:** the model received something other than the managed denial. On certified 2.2.0 that is produced just as readily by calls upstream rejects before the hook runs (`Tool \"LS\" not found`, `Invalid args for tool …`, the sensitive-path `PathSecurityError` for `.env`, per-tool resolve errors, `Tool skipped because a previous tool call stopped the turn.`), by a coexisting PreToolUse hook ahead of the managed block or an upstream permission policy blocking first, or by a cancel/budget abort landing before the result — none of which executed anything — as by a hook that failed open. Because the stream carries no outcome field, the plugin cannot tell these apart, so it reports and does not fail: the job completes or fails on its own merits, `status`/`result --json` carry `hook_escapes`, stderr prints a `safety hook notice`, and the review gate annotates `systemMessage` without changing its decision. Treat a finding as a prompt to run `/kimi:setup --check` and read the excerpt, not as proof of a breach; treat a *recurring* `mismatch` whose excerpt looks like tool output (`Wrote N bytes to …`) as a drifted hook. Coverage is streamed calls under read-only labels and pure denials under write labels — not filesystem-dependent rescue allowlist decisions, not swarm subagent calls (in-process, never streamed). Non-vacuous live control (CLI 2.2.0, 2026-10-15): with the hook command pointed at a nonexistent script upstream failed open, `Write` created the file, and the finding was `mismatch` with excerpt `Wrote 7 bytes to ESCAPE.txt`; with the hook intact the same prompt produced the byte-exact denial and no finding. Enforcement (stopping the run, failing the job) is deliberately not shipped: it needs positive execution evidence. The upstream ask, filed as MoonshotAI/kimi-code#4241, is an `outcome: executed|vetoed|rejected` field on print-mode tool records; a plugin-side alternative is a per-job trace the hook writes before it exits.\n\n## Review-gate thinking request\n\nThe gate requests `off` through `KIMI_MODEL_THINKING_EFFORT` by default. `KIMI_PLUGIN_CC_REVIEW_GATE_THINKING=inherit` leaves the ambient environment alone; any other non-empty value matching `/^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{0,31}$/` is passed verbatim. This is best-effort, never an enforced latency guarantee: non-trait-driven/BYO providers ignore it silently, an already-off base remains off, and an always-thinking model receives `off` unnormalized and may continue reasoning. Stream-json has no thinking deltas, so honouring the request cannot be observed. The 8 s budget and fail-open-on-timeout contract are unchanged; a hook-escape finding only annotates the gate's `systemMessage`. `KIMI_PLUGIN_CC_REVIEW_GATE_THINKING` is lowercased like `--thinking`.\n"

      "path": "plugins/kimi-dsh/README.md",
      "content": "# kimi-plugin-cc for DeepSeek Harness\n\nKimi Code subagents for DeepSeek Harness (DSH), backed by the same companion runtime as the Claude Code and Codex plugins.\n\n## What this bundle provides\n\n| Tool | Operation | File access |\n|---|---|---|\n| `kimi_ask` | Answer a self-contained repository question | Read-only |\n| `kimi_review` | Review the working tree, including untracked files | Read-only |\n| `kimi_challenge` | Challenge assumptions and design choices | Read-only |\n| `kimi_rescue` | Investigate and implement a bounded fix | Can edit the selected workspace |\n| `kimi_pursue` | Pursue an autonomous multi-turn objective with a finite budget | Can edit the selected workspace |\n| `kimi_swarm` | Fan out independent read-only subagents | Read-only |\n| `kimi_swarm_write` | Edit disjoint targets in a temporary worktree and return a patch | Patch only; never applies or commits |\n\nEvery activation starts a fresh companion and Kimi CLI process. The existing runtime owns hook verification, exact Kimi-version certification, SQLite jobs, response or safety budgets, artifacts, and process teardown. DSH owns delegation identity and completion notices. Parent conversations do not flow into the child, and child tool traffic stays out of the parent conversation.\n\nJob controls are `/kimi-status [job-id]`, `/kimi-result [job-id]`, and `/kimi-cancel [job-id]`. Without an id, status and result select the latest job for the current repository, and cancel selects the latest active job. Cancellation stops work but does not roll back changes or patches already produced.\n\n## Requirements\n\n- Node.js 24.9.0 or later.\n- DeepSeek Harness >=0.2.1-rc.5 <0.3.0; this package is developed and composed against 0.2.1-rc.5.\n- Kimi Code CLI on `PATH`, authenticated and configured through Kimi. The companion's exact-version certification table remains authoritative.\n- A patched DSH host and profiles with zod >=4.6.6 and undici >=8.12.2; see [host installation and audit instructions](../../docs/registry-releases.md#patched-dsh-host-and-profiles). The plugin does not patch your host automatically.\n\n## Install\n\nFrom this repository checkout:\n\n```sh\ndsh plugin --profile web add ./plugins/kimi-dsh\n```\n\nFor another DSH profile, replace `web` with its name. To install the published root package instead, run `dsh plugin --profile web add kimi-plugin-cc`.\n\nFor DSH Discover, enable **Custom plugin indexes** and add `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/linxule/kimi-plugin-cc/main/dsh/index.json` as an index source.\n\nRestart when requested, then run `/kimi-setup`. Setup is explicit: installing or enabling the bundle does not modify Kimi configuration. Delegation refuses to start when the DSH managed hook is missing or invalid.\n\nUseful setup commands:\n\n```text\n/kimi-setup --check\n/kimi-setup --models\n/kimi-setup --models --json\n/kimi-setup --uninstall\n```\n\nModel inventory is local and credential-safe; it is not a connection test. Uninstall removes only the DSH managed block. The all-host `--uninstall --all` action is deliberately not exposed through the DSH command.\n\n## Use\n\nAsk DSH to use one of the seven tools with a self-contained task. Each accepts a description, prompt, and optional working directory, returns an activation id, and delivers the final result when the companion finishes. Review and challenge treat the prompt as focus text. Pursue and swarm operations retain their existing finite default budgets; swarm-write returns the captured patch path without applying it.\n\nPrefer `/kimi-cancel` for stopping work when possible. DSH cancellation also terminates the managed subprocess range and waits for quiescence.\n\n## Configuration\n\nThe bundle's `kimi-plugin-cc` row accepts:\n\n| Field | Default | Meaning |\n|---|---|---|\n| `dataRoot` | `$DSH_HOME/plugin-data/kimi-plugin-cc` | Absolute companion data directory; `KIMI_PLUGIN_CC_DATA` overrides the derived default |\n| `env` | `{}` | Explicit child environment layered over DSH's credential-scrubbed environment |\n| `disposeGraceMs` | `6000` | Managed subprocess termination grace in milliseconds; minimum 6000 |\n| `maxOutputBytes` | `16777216` | Maximum captured stdout or stderr bytes per command |\n| `model` | Native Kimi default | Optional configured model alias applied to every delegation |\n| `thinkingEffort` | Native Kimi default | Optional per-run thinking effort request |\n| `budget` | Existing command default | Optional duration such as `30m`, `1h`, or `90s`, validated at load and capped at 24h |\n| `reviewBase` | Working tree | Optional Git base applied only to review and challenge |\n\nHost identity, workspace, hook path, Node binary, and bypass variables are provider-owned and cannot be replaced through `env`. The DSH managed block uses host id `dsh`; Claude Code and Codex blocks remain independent. Native Kimi authentication and provider configuration stay under `KIMI_CODE_HOME` or `~/.kimi-code`.\n\n## Limits\n\n- Activations are one-shot and do not accept follow-up input, parent-context inheritance, per-call model overrides, output schemas, or Harness depth enforcement. Use profile configuration for a fixed model or thinking request; interactive ask/rescue resume stays outside the DSH provider.\n- DSH activation ids are not companion job ids. Use the slash commands to inspect companion state.\n- There is no child progress stream. Response-time budgets, safety ceilings, and timeout artifacts follow the existing companion rules.\n- The parent receives final stdout only on success. stderr stays on the host; failures use bounded diagnostics without task text, credentials, or raw protocol payloads.\n- This package does not create an account, select a provider, repair Kimi authentication, or provide an approval channel beyond the companion's managed PreToolUse policy.\n- Rescue and pursue edit the real selected workspace. Swarm-write works from born HEAD in a temporary worktree, excludes uncommitted changes, and returns a patch without applying or committing it.\n"

reason: string }> = [];\n  // Rolling stderr tail — keep only the trailing STDERR_TAIL_BYTES so a\n  // long-running kimi process emitting megabytes of stderr (tool.progress,\n  // thinking deltas) doesn't grow our RSS unboundedly.\n  let stderrTail = \"\";\n  let announcedSessionId: string | undefined;\n  let announcedGoalSummary: GoalSummaryRecord | undefined;\n  let announcedCliError: CliErrorRecord | undefined;\n  let announcedSystemVersion: string | undefined;\n  const hookMonitor = createHookEscapeMonitor({ commandLabel: opts.commandLabel,\n    operationKind: opts.executionPlan.operationKind, trustedWorkspaceRoot: opts.trustedWorkspaceRoot, cwd: opts.cwd });\n  const hookEscapes: HookEscape[] = [];\n  const noteHookEscape = (escape: HookEscape) => {\n    hookEscapes.push(escape);\n    appendLogLine({ event: \"hook_escape\", ...escape, command_label: opts.commandLabel,\n      operation_kind: opts.executionPlan.operationKind });\n  };\n  let engineMismatchDetected = false;\n  let handleEngineMismatch: ((mismatch: EngineMismatch) => void) | undefined;\n  const plannedEngine = opts.executionPlan.intendedEngine;\n  const plannedVersion =\n    opts.executionPlan.kimiVersion === null\n      ? null\n      : (parseVersionLine(opts.executionPlan.kimiVersion)?.raw ?? opts.executionPlan.kimiVersion);\n  let logChain: Promise<void> = Promise.resolve();\n\n  const appendLogLine = (payload: Record<string, unknown>) => {\n    if (opts.logPath === undefined) return;\n    const line = `${JSON.stringify({ ts: new Date().toISOString(), ...payload })}\\n`;\n    logChain = logChain.then(() =>\n      appendFile(opts.logPath!, line, \"utf8\").catch(() => {\n        // Diagnostics best-effort; A multi-line or\n            // otherwise decorated value must not be normalized into a certified\n            // one by taking its first line.\n            const observedVersion = parseExactVersionToken(outcome.record.version);\n            if (observedVersion === undefined) {\n              handleEngineMismatch?.({\n                observedEngine: \"native-v2\",\n                systemVersion: outcome.record.version,\n                reason: `the system.version marker carries a malformed version value ${JSON.stringify(outcome.record.version)}; the started engine's version cannot be established.`,\n              });\n              return;\n            }\n            if (plannedVersion !== null && observedVersion !== plannedVersion) {\n              handleEngineMismatch?.({\n                observedEngine: \"native-v2\",\n                systemVersion: outcome.record.version,\n                reason: `the system.version marker reports ${outcome.record.version}, but the plan certified ${plannedVersion}.`,\n              });\n              return;\n            }\n          }\n          continue;\n        }\n        if (requireMarkerBeforeOutput(`a ${outcome.record.role} record`)) return;\n        const escape = hookMonitor.observe(outcome.record);\n        if (escape) noteHookEscape(escape);\n        records.push(outcome.record);\n        appendLogLine({ event: \"record\", record: outcome.record });\n        invokeOnRecord(outcome.record);\n      } else if (outcome.malformedLine !== undefined) {\n        // Diagnostics-only in general, but on a native-v2 plan a line that is\n        // not the marker arriving first still violates marker-first: the\n        // engine that produced it cannot be established.\n        if (requireMarkerBeforeOutput(\"a malformed stream-json line\")) return;\n        const entry = {\n          line: truncateChars(outcome.malformedLine, 200),\n          reason: outcome.malformedReason ??
